learn.title: Same job, two styles
learn.body: Anything you write with recursion you can write with a loop, and the reverse. Loops keep their state in variables. Recursion keeps it in the arguments of each call. Which to use depends on clarity and cost.

learn.title: Fibonacci with a loop
learn.body: Two variables hold the last two numbers. The loop slides them forward. It does n additions: $O(n)$.

learn.title: The cost of repeated work
learn.body: The recursive fib recomputes the same values again and again. `fib(10)` makes 177 calls. `fib(30)` makes 2,692,537 calls, while the loop above does 30 steps. For this problem the loop is enormously faster.

learn.title: The stack
learn.body: Each recursive call that is still waiting holds memory. A loop uses the same few variables however long it runs. A very deep recursion, say a million levels, can overflow the stack, and a loop would not.

learn.title: When recursion shines
learn.body: Recursion is natural when the problem has a self-similar shape: halving a range, merge sort, walking a tree. There the recursive code is short and clear, and the work per call is small. Use a loop when the loop is just as clear.

learn.title: Choosing a style
steps: Sum 1 to n: a loop is simple and uses no stack
fib(n): a loop avoids the repeated work
Binary search: recursion or a loop both work well
Sorting by splitting in halves: recursion reads best

questions.prompt: How many calls does the naive recursive `fib(10)` make?
questions.explanation: Counting the calls by running the code gives 177.

questions.prompt: How many additions does the loop version of `fib(30)` do?
questions.explanation: One addition per loop pass, and the loop runs 30 times.

choices: It recomputes the same values many times
questions.explanation: For example, `fib(2)` is computed again and again inside `fib(4)`.

questions.prompt: Each waiting recursive call uses memory on the \_\_.

questions.explanation: Self-similar problems turn into short recursive functions.

questions.prompt: A loop and recursion both compute the same answer. Which statement is true?
choices: Either is correct, so cost and clarity decide
questions.explanation: They are equally powerful, so choose by clarity and cost.

questions.prompt: Match each style to its state.
questions.explanation: The two styles hold their working data in different places.
